Apnea of prematurity is the most common cause in preterm infants <44 weeks postmenstrual age and remains plausible even in late preterm or early term infants with immature respiratory control; its high frequency and progression align with the clinical description (confidence 0.85). Central sleep apnea reflects failure of brainstem respiratory drive and may occur idiopathically or secondary to neurological immaturity or injury (0.78). Obstructive sleep apnea, though less common in young infants than older children, can arise from craniofacial anomalies, hypotonia, or upper airway narrowing—and may present with paradoxical breathing or snorting (0.72). Laryngomalacia is the most frequent cause of stridor and obstructive symptoms in infancy and can cause intermittent apnea, especially supine or during feeding/sleep, often worsening over first few months (0.65). Seizure-related apnea (e.g., in benign familial neonatal-infantile seizures or epileptic encephalopathies) is less common but must be considered when apnea lacks clear respiratory triggers, occurs with associated cyanosis, eye deviation, or posturing, and shows no response to stimulation—though absence of other seizure features lowers likelihood (0.58). Obstructive sleep apnea is highly plausible given its prevalence in infants with upper airway anomalies (e.g., laryngomalacia), and the absence of chest/abdominal movement data prevents ruling it out. Apnea of prematurity remains likely if gestational age <37 weeks—even if corrected age is >44 weeks—as apnea can persist. Breath-holding spells typically occur in response to distress or pain while awake or drowsy—not truly asleep—and lack respiratory effort during events, making them less likely but not impossible in atypical presentations. CCHS is rare (<1:200,000) and usually presents with profound hypoventilation in wakefulness and sleep, often with autonomic dysregulation (e.g., Hirschsprung disease, abnormal pupillary responses); low confidence reflects rarity and requirement for PHOX2B testing. Diagnostic uncertainty is moderate (entropy ~1.52), reflecting substantial overlap in presentation and critical missing data (e.g., gestational age, oxygen saturation, cardiorespiratory monitoring, feeding history, neurologic exam)."}
